prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my single preferred part, with Katori and Ye. After the full exchange, six members prefer it with an identical two-name credit, and no one has argued that the science is wrong. I do not count that as a reason in itself. What persuades me is that the three tests I apply, a concrete discovery, secure confirmation and clean credit, all hold here at once. The new idea is state-insensitive trapping of thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, which removes the trade-off between statistical gain and trap-induced shifts. Ye's group then showed that this could be turned into systematic control near 1e-18 together with many-body coherence. Independent laboratories reproduce the performance with Sr and Yb, and the clocks are compared across continents. That answers the chair's first question: the citation should name the lattice, the neutral atoms and the accuracy, and should not mention frequency metrology in general. That wording separates it from the 2005 comb, which supplied the counting clockwork, and from the 2012 single-quantum-system control, which concerned individual ions.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against is still distinctness. A third precision-frequency prize in about twenty-five years could look like a continuation of a line the Academy has already honoured, and Eriksson and Mehlig are right that the conceptual break is smaller than for a new platform of correlated matter. Second, a two-name prize leaves out Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto and the PTB, NIST and Paris groups. I have not verified the priority chronology from primary sources and I am relying on general knowledge, as several colleagues are, so the chair's second question remains open for me. Third, the redefinition of the second is pending, so some of the consequences are prospective. I accept the first two as real costs. I do not accept the third as a reason to wait, because the discovery is the demonstrated and reproduced accuracy.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, argues that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is a long prediction-to-confirmation chain, and says a lattice clock prize would be the third precision-frequency prize in twenty-five years.
responses.response: I take the second point seriously, and I have changed my wording because of it, though not my ranking. I now think the citation must say neutral atoms at a magic wavelength and not optical frequency standards in general. On B013, your argument that a citation resting on flat bands and the correlated phases, not the pairing mechanism, avoids the maturity objection is a fair answer to the chair's fourth question, and I accept it for that purpose. Two things remain for me. The Andrei question is a priority judgment that neither of us has settled, and the 2010 and 2016 condensed-matter prizes lie nearby in subject. The prediction was 2011 and the experiment 2018, but twist-angle disorder and uneven reproducibility still make the phase diagram less stable than a clock comparison that anyone can repeat. I would support B013 if the room moves that way, and I would want Andrei's exclusion stated openly.

responses.point: Mehlig says B013 is the more novel discovery, and that B001 is the safer choice if the committee weighs maturity above novelty.
responses.response: I agree that is the real choice, and I put maturity and clean credit first when two cases are both scientifically sound. I did not change on this, but you have shown me that the test is not obviously neutral. If the committee weights conceptual novelty more, B013 is a defensible outcome. Your caution that any B013 citation should be conservative about the phase diagram because of sample variability is also one I share. On the Andrei point I side with you and Eriksson against Pearce's opening substitution. Bistritzer and MacDonald co-wrote the continuum model, and removing one of them to make room is harder to defend than naming Andrei's STM work in the discussion. I would also answer your doubt about overlap in this way: the lattice clock is a different solution to the stability problem, not a refinement of the comb or of ion control, but I accept that the case for a conceptual break is smaller than for moire matter.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a different solution to the stability problem and concedes that Hall's link to the earlier prize makes B001 look more like a continuation than he first said, so the citation should be about the lattice.
responses.response: I agree with your conclusion and I have adopted your suggestion in my citation. I would add that your disclosed stay in Hall's laboratory is a reasonable thing to weigh when you judge distinctness, and I note that you made the point against the continuation reading anyway, which reassures me. On the early-credit question, I agree that Katori should anchor the citation. I would not add Lemonde or the Tokyo and Paris groups to a three-name cap, because that would require a chronology none of us has checked. Whether the chronology should change the two names is the one item I would still like checked by a member who has read the primary papers.

responses.point: Olsson says the citation for lattice clocks has to say what is new, namely many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength averaging down statistically to 1e-18, and keeps B013 as her first alternative.
responses.response: This is the wording I now use, and I think your formulation is the best answer so far to the chair's first question. I also noted your concern that a citation should not hide that the redefinition is pending or that other groups contributed. I would not put the redefinition in the citation, because that would tie our text to a body outside physics. I would be comfortable with the committee's public description stating that others contributed to the lattice clock record. Your experimentalist's point that systematics control is what turns a proposal into a standard is the part of the argument that I find most convincing on maturity.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether the third precision-frequency prize in about twenty-five years is still acceptable.
The early priority chronology for lattice clocks (Lemonde, Ido, Takamoto, PTB, NIST, Paris) which I have not checked in primary papers, and whether it would alter the credited names.

If the committee turns to B013, whether naming Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero with Andrei's exclusion stated openly would be accepted as fair, and whether a citation that avoids the pairing mechanism removes the maturity concern.
Whether a topological-insulator prize can be scoped to three names while leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and either Mele or Hasan.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B013 or B024. My documented connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) lie in string theory and cosmology and none involves a shortlisted name. I note Kroll's disclosed stay in Hall's laboratory and Johansson's declared recusal on B029, and I treat Eriksson's comment on DMFT as irrelevant to this configuration. As a theorist outside atomic physics I am relying on colleagues' expertise for the lattice-clock chronology.
